title: Optimal Intermediate Hamiltonians for Non-Equilibrium Free Energy Calculations: A Numerical Study of Markov Models
abstract: The Jarzynski relation enables the estimation of equilibrium free energy differences from non-equilibrium, finite-time switching simulations. These estimates usually converge poorly because rare trajectories dominate the exponential work average. Here, we numerically determined and explored the sequence of intermediate Hamiltonians connecting initial and final states that minimize the mean squared error (MSE) of the Jarzynski estimator and thereby enhance convergence. For discrete-time Markov models, an exact tilted-master-equation representation of the MSE in the large-sample limit, combined with automatic differentiation, enables efficient gradient-based minimization over all intermediate energies. We applied our approach to three model systems of increasing complexity: a two-state model, a double-well potential, and a shifted potential well. In all three systems, the optimal intermediate Hamiltonians jump at the initial and final times. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations show that optimal intermediates can reduce the MSE by more than an order of magnitude compared with linear and logarithmic interpolation, most strongly for large changes in the energy landscape. Remarkably, they need not dissipate less work than intermediates yielding larger errors. Our results suggest heuristics for more efficient non-equilibrium free energy calculations of realistic molecular systems: optimal intermediate Hamiltonians jump at the initial and final times; for barrier-crossing problems, the barrier should be lowered rapidly and raised again later; and minimizing dissipation does not guarantee faster convergence.
summary: This work introduces a method to optimize the intermediate Hamiltonians used in non-equilibrium free energy calculations, specifically targeting the convergence issues of the Jarzynski estimator. By minimizing the Mean Squared Error (MSE) using gradient-based optimization on Markov models, the authors show that optimal Hamiltonians drastically improve accuracy. This provides valuable heuristics for simulating complex physical processes where rare events dominate the work average.
main_problem: The paper addresses the poor convergence of the Jarzynski estimator when estimating equilibrium free energy differences from non-equilibrium, finite-time switching simulations.
main_result: Optimal intermediate Hamiltonians significantly reduce the Mean Squared Error (MSE) of the Jarzynski estimator by more than an order of magnitude compared to simple interpolation schemes.
method: The authors developed a gradient-based minimization technique using an exact tilted-master-equation representation of the MSE for discrete-time Markov models.
model_or_system: The study utilizes discrete-time Markov models with a finite state space arranged on a line, governed by a time-dependent Hamiltonian $H(x, 	au)$ and evolving via a master equation.
key_observables: Mean Squared Error (MSE) of the Jarzynski estimator, mean work $\langle W angle$, and mean position $\langle x angle$.
important_parameters: System size ($m$), potential well depth ($\delta$), number of intermediates ($N$), and time steps ($	au$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on approximating the MSE in the large-sample limit and assumes the Jarzynski relation holds for the chosen Markov dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures systematically compare the structure of optimal vs. linear/logarithmic intermediate Hamiltonians across varying system parameters, and correlation plots show MSE and mean work comparisons.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical framework (Jarzynski relation, MSE minimization) to applying the optimization technique to various model systems (two-state, double-well, shifted potential) and rigorously benchmarking the optimal Hamiltonians against standard interpolation methods.
why_interesting: The methodology provides a powerful, generalizable framework for improving non-equilibrium calculations, which is crucial for simulating processes like reaction rates or work extraction in complex quantum or molecular systems.
